sheet.opening: Vesper Thorne, a violet-skinned tiefling bard and con artist (chaotic neutral, CHA 17, rapier, lute, Sleep, Charm Person, Disguise Self, Faerie Fire, Vicious Mockery, Minor Illusion), is a level-1 character. Backstory (must stay true): found as a toddler in a fish crate on the steps of the shabby Shrine of the Lantern Saint in the river town of Marrowmere; raised by overworked Sister Odalie, who taught her scripture and never quite caught her stealing, and who gave her her first silk scarf (Vesper keeps that scarf in her pack always, never parted with, even while wearing newer scarves over her curling horns). Vesper worked the pews on feast days, then market stalls. At sixteen she left in the night with the shrine's silver offering bowl, never sold it, still carries it polished in her pack, and means to return it someday; the debt to Odalie is bigger than the bowl. Ideal: freedom, no one writes her script. Flaw: cannot resist a mark too sure of themselves even when walking away is smarter. Her tail twitches when she lies so she keeps it tucked under her coat; gold eyes look too honest. She never tells the same story twice and will cheat anyone but never a friend. Carries 15 gp, leather armor, rapier, dagger, lute, a stolen reliquary bearing another faith's saint, an annotated prayer book. Opening suggestion: Vesper is on the road some days from Marrowmere, arriving at the river-crossing village of Hollin Ford at dusk, mid-con, working a loud, overconfident merchant (exactly the kind of mark she can't resist) at the ferry inn with a fake relic story, when a wounded courier stumbles in clutching a sealed satchel and a message that names the Shrine of the Lantern Saint, or news arrives that Marrowmere's river shrine is in trouble. Something has just happened that pulls both her con and her unpaid debt to Odalie into the story, and forces her to choose between cheating the mark and acting. Invent all further names, places and details; use only SRD-compatible creatures and magic.

The river country of the Marrow Reach is a land of slow brown water, reed-choked fords and small shrines to saints nobody quite remembers. Travelers keep to the riverside roads. The road, as always, is where the coin is.

Vesper Thorne is violet-skinned, gold-eyed and curl-horned, and she wears a silk scarf over those horns. She was a fish-crate foundling raised by Sister Odalie at the Shrine of the Lantern Saint in Marrowmere. She left at sixteen with the shrine's silver offering bowl, which she has never sold and still polishes. Now she's some days upriver with fifteen gold, a rapier, a lute and a talent for stories.

Dusk settles over Hollin Ford. The Drowned Lantern, the ferry inn, is warm with smoke and lamplight, and the river mutters against the pilings outside. At the best table sits Corvin Aldersey, a wool merchant in a green cloak, loud and red-faced, with a fat purse he keeps patting. For half an hour you've been spinning him the tale of a holy finger bone of "Saint Brannoc." He's sweating, he's leaning in, and he's nearly sold. "Fifty gold, you say? For a saint? Hah! I've paid more for worse!"

Then the inn door bangs open. A courier in a mud-caked river-warden's tabard staggers in, clutching a sealed satchel to a bleeding side. His eyes sweep the room and land on your lute, your horns and your face. "Lantern..." he rasps. "The Lantern Saint's shrine. Marrowmere. Is anyone here from... Is there anyone..." He sags against a post, and the room goes quiet.

Corvin has a hand on your sleeve, his purse already open. "Well? Do we have a deal, girl?"

What does Vesper do?

Vesper slides Corvin's hand off her sleeve with a warm pat and a murmured, "Hold that thought, friend, the saint will keep a minute." She gets up, tucks her tail under her coat, and crosses to the courier fast, kneeling beside him and keeping her voice low and steady. "I'm from the Lantern Saint's shrine, Marrowmere, Sister Odalie raised me. Easy now, who sent you, and what's in the satchel?"

The wax cracks cleanly, and the lantern stamp stays in one piece. Inside the satchel are three things.

The first is a letter in Odalie's cramped, familiar hand, the same hand that wrote your name in the shrine ledger when you were small. The second is a brass key shaped like a lantern, as long as your palm and cold, heavier than it should be. The third is a stoppered glass vial of pale oil. In the barge lantern's light it doesn't reflect the flame. It holds a small, steady glow of its own.

The letter reads:

*Vesper. If this has reached you, then Tamsin is a better courier than I deserved. I know about the bowl. I always knew. Keep it. That is not why I write. Under the shrine is the undercroft the old Lantern Keepers sealed, and what sleeps there is not a relic to be sold. Men have come who know its name. The key opens the door, and the Saint's Flame keeps what lies behind it quiet. Don't give them either. Don't come back for me if it means the door opens. Come back for the door. — Odalie*

Below it, in a shakier line: *You were never a thief to me, child. You were a lantern left on the step.*

The barge creaks. Tamsin stirs but doesn't wake. Corvin watches from the stern and pretends not to.

What does Vesper do?

Vesper reads the last line twice, then folds the letter against her chest and pulls Odalie's old scarf from her pack to hold in her fist for a moment. She slips the key and the glowing vial back into the satchel, buckles it under her coat, and murmurs to the sleeping Tamsin, "She knew about the bowl, warden. All this time." Then she lifts her voice toward the stern, easy and bright. "Corvin, how long till Marrowmere on the morning tide, and does your *Plump Heron* have any trick for running faster in the dark?"

Corvin sniffs, glad to be asked something he knows. "Trick? She's a wool barge, girl, not a racehorse. Current does the work. Two deckhands on the poles, me at the tiller. A barge sitting dark across it would take little effort to hold."

The deckhands trade a look. One of them, a thin man called Piet, spits over the side. "River's been quiet tonight. Too quiet. No frogs."

Two hours slide past under a thin moon. The reeds hiss, Tamsin sleeps, and the lantern at the prow throws a small gold circle on the water. Then ahead, past the bend, you see the faintest smudge of orange: a covered lantern, shuttered nearly shut, hanging low on a dark shape that lies across the channel.

Piet hisses, "Barge. Dark. Right in the Bend."

Corvin's hand goes white on the tiller. "Saints preserve us. Do we turn?"

The current is carrying you toward it. What does Vesper do?

Vesper is on her feet at once, hand on her rapier. "Don't turn, Corvin, and don't slow. Douse our prow lantern and bring us in dark and quiet, like a barge with nothing to hide." She quietly weaves a Minor Illusion in her mind: "Piet, can you see any crew on that deck, and how many poles do they have in the water?"

Tamsin gets one foot over the side of the pallet, goes grey, and sits back down hard. "Walk, yes. Fast, no." He grips the bale and tries a crooked smile. "Mags's place. I'll hold the door and tell the Reeve what I saw. Carrying a message is the one thing I'm still good for."

Nobody is on the landing but a gaunt dog. Piet and Corvin lower Tamsin between them, and he leans his weight on your shoulder. Together you take the steps toward the streets. Up on the hill, the smoke is thicker, and a single bell is tolling, slow and uneven, as if someone is ringing it by hand and getting tired.

Vesper steers Tamsin down the side lane toward Eel Row first, keeping the hood low, and knocks softly on Old Mags's door. "Mags, it's Odalie's girl, the one with the horns. I've brought you a wounded warden and I need to know who's on that hill before I climb it."

The door opens a crack on a chain, and one rheumy eye studies you through it. "Hm. The one who took the bowl." The chain rattles free. "In, in, and mind the nets. You've grown. Still too thin."

Old Mags is a stooped woman with forearms like mooring rope. She takes Tamsin's weight without a word and lays him on a cot of fishing-floats and sacking, and she doesn't ask how he got hurt. She talks as she works, flat and fast.

"Came last night, a dozen or more, off the river with no lights. Took the shrine yard before the bell rang. Odalie barred the sanctuary and the cellar stair and has been ringing the bell by hand since dawn, so the town knows she's alive. Sorrel Thack and two of the watch are at the foot of the hill road, saying it's *for order*." She spits. "They set the woodshed alight to smoke her out, and it's gone to a smoulder. She jerks her chin toward the back window and the dark slope behind it. "The front way's shut. But there's a Pilgrims' Water-Stair, from the old days when they came up by boat for the Lantern feast. Silence. Three slow knocks and one quick, and on the far side of the door the breathing stops entirely.

Then the bar scrapes, slowly, with an old woman's care, and the door opens a hand's width onto candlelight. Sister Odalie is smaller than you remember. Her grey habit is soot-streaked, there's a cut over one eye and a bruise on her jaw, and her hands, which once scrubbed a hundred pews, tremble on the rope-rough bar. Her eyes are still the same pale, tired grey.

She doesn't say your name. She looks at the violet of your skin and the curl of your horns beneath the hood, the way she looked at you once on a step in a fish crate, and her mouth works.

"You stole the good beeswax too," she says at last, very low. "Last winter. I thought it was the rats." She tries to smile and it cracks. Her hand comes through the gap and finds your sleeve, and holds it as if you might evaporate. "Child. The key. Tamsin got through?"

Behind her the sanctuary is dim: overturned benches, a barricaded front door, the bell rope hanging from the loft, and the undercroft's iron-bound door in the floor of the side chapel. Outside, Ashgrove's calm voice is giving orders again.

What does Vesper do?

Vesper slips through the gap, catches Odalie's trembling hand in both of hers, and nods, tail curling around her leg for once. "He got through, Sister. He's alive at Old Mags's, and I have the key and the Saint's Flame, but you're hurt, so sit before you fall." She glances at the iron-bound door in the chapel floor. "And I'll still say it: I stole the beeswax, I took your silver bowl, and I'm sorry. Now tell me fast what's actually sleeping under there, and what Ashgrove wants it for."

Odalie lets herself be lowered onto a pew, one hand still gripping yours. When she speaks, the tiredness drops away and the sister you remember comes back, the one who explained scripture the way you'd explain a coin trick.

"Before there was a town, there was a drowned thing. A wyrm, green as river-weed and old as the first flood, that came up the Marrow and took villages in its sleep. The first Lantern Keepers couldn't kill it. So they put it back to sleep in the mud and built a shrine on top, and bound it with two things: the lantern key and a lamp that never goes out." Her eyes flick to your coat. "The Saint's Flame. As long as it burns in the undercroft, the Sleeper sleeps. But the lamp is old, child. The oil's nearly gone. I was going to refill it, and then *she* came."

She breathes. "Ashgrove doesn't want the treasure there, because there isn't any. She wants the wyrm. A beast like that obeys whoever holds its key and says the old words at the new moon. Nine nights." A bitter laugh. "She asked politely for the key, you know. Over tea. I told her I'd already given it to a fish."

Outside, Ashgrove's voice has paused. A boot scrapes on the front step. Then a knock on the sanctuary door, three polite raps. "Sister Odalie," the voice calls, pleasantly. "I do hope you've had time to reconsider. I'd so hate to have to burn the rest of your house."

input.add_to_description: Undercroft: vaulted stone chamber, water channel around the wyrm, bronze lamp pillar at the stair foot. A narrow Keepers' gallery runs off the east wall, a service tunnel that climbs behind the hill and joins the Water-Stair at the landing beneath the carved lantern arch. Vesper locked the undercroft door from inside with the brass key.

transcript.text: notebook: updated The Sleeper

The key turns with a deep, satisfying clunk, and the iron-bound door is locked from your side. Above, the ram's last blow rings off the chapel floor. A silence follows, then the polite voice again, nearer: "A very small candle, Miss Thorne? You'll find I'm patient. I have a whole night, and a nine-night after that."

She knows your name. The door is old iron and oak, banded, and it will hold for a time. The ram will not get through it quickly, but she has a dozen men and a night.

You turn your back on it and make a slow circuit of the vault, giving the great closed eye a wide berth. The lamp's gold light shows the walls clearly now. Carved lanterns march around the chamber in a frieze, each with a name beneath. Your own would fit among them, you think, with a small shock. On the east wall, half-hidden behind a pillar of black stone, is a low arch you'd miss if you weren't looking: a narrow Keepers' gallery, ankle-deep in cold water, sloping upward into the hill. A breath of river air comes from it, and far away you can hear the faint drip of the Water-Stair.

Behind you the Sleeper breathes in, and out. The lamp holds steady. Above, men are shouting. You have the key in your hand, the satchel across your back, and the town's bell still echoing in your ears.

What does Vesper do?

Vesper tucks the key safely into her satchel and drops her voice to a whisper. "Thank you for the quiet, big fellow, I'll try not to wake you." She wades into the Keepers' gallery, keeping the lamp's gold at her back, and follows the river air up toward the Water-Stair to catch Odalie and find the Reeve before Ashgrove thinks to circle the hill.

"DM: when I get out, can I still hear the bell in town, and is Brannoc Vell's watch answering it yet?"

input.add_to_description: Answered the shrine bell with the harbour watch, marching up the hill road with torches and a few dozen townsfolk, over Deputy Sorrel Thack's objections.

transcript.text: notebook: updated Brannoc Vell

The gallery climbs in a long, cold dark, ankle-deep and slick underfoot. Twice you duck under low stone. The air grows fresher, with river and tar in it, and then the Water-Stair opens beside you at the landing under the carved lantern arch, exactly where you passed it an hour ago. The sleeping bandits' torchlight glints through the cellar grate above. Both men are still trussed, and one of them now looks at you with a very worried face.

You can hear the bell. It isn't Odalie's now. It's the old iron bell of the Grand Quay and the chapel bells of three other streets, picking up the alarm one by one, and under that is a rising roar of voices. Down through the arch of the stair mouth you can see torchlight on the hill road, a long wavering line of it. It's the harbour watch, perhaps twenty of them, with fishermen, tanners and net-menders behind, armed with boathooks, cleavers and cudgels. At the head of them strides a broad, grey-bearded man in a Reeve's chain, bellowing for Deputy Thack. Thack, two paces behind with a very pale face, is not answering.

Ashgrove's men are on the shrine's front step. You count at least ten, and no one has sounded a horn yet. Ashgrove herself is nowhere you can see, and the camp chair is empty.

At the bottom of the stair, in the lee of the net-sheds, a stooped figure in a grey habit waves from Mags's back door. Odalie. Tamsin's pale face looks out beside her.

What does Vesper do?

Vesper slips down the stair into the lee of the net-sheds, pulls Odalie into a quick fierce hug, then peels the oilcloth hood back so the Reeve will see her real face. "Sister, stay with Tamsin and bar Mags's door. I'm taking Ashgrove's orders and Thack's pay-chit straight to Brannoc Vell before that deputy can open his mouth."

input.add_to_description: Convinced by Vesper with Ashgrove's orders and Thack's pay-chit; arrested Deputy Sorrel Thack and stopped at the shrine's front gate with the watch and townsfolk, facing Ashgrove's men. The standoff now holds at the shrine yard.

transcript.text: notebook: updated Brannoc Vell

Odalie's arms are thin but fierce around you, and she smells of tallow and smoke. "Go," she says into your shoulder. "And Vesper... you were never a thief to me." Then she pushes you away and shuts Mags's door.

You think of the hood and realize your face is still hers. You take one breath to dismiss the illusion, and the old woman's features slide from you like water. You are violet and horned again.

The hill road is a river of torches. Brannoc Vell stands at the foot of the shrine gate with the harbour watch ranked behind him, grey-bearded and furious. Ashgrove's men hold the yard behind a line of overturned handcarts, crossbows leveled. Thack hovers behind the Reeve with his hat in his hands.

You walk straight up the middle of the road, hands open, with the pay-chit held high where the torchlight can read it. The Reeve's eyes go from the deputy's mark to your face, and for a moment you see the dock-warrant look in his eyes. Then you hold out Ashgrove's orders. *Take the key by the third night. The old woman is not to be harmed.* He reads, and his jaw works. He reads the pay-chit, and turns his head very slowly toward his own deputy.

"Sorrel," he says, without raising his voice. "Your belt, if you please."

Thack's mouth opens. No sound comes out. Two watchmen, who until a minute ago called him sir, take his arms. The crowd behind them growls.

Across the yard, behind the carts, a white-gloved hand lifts in a polite, almost friendly wave. Ashgrove has reappeared, in the open doorway of the sanctuary she failed to break, with a thin smile.

"Miss Thorne," she calls, clear and pleasant over the crowd. "You've made quite a night of it. Shall we talk?"

The Reeve's watch, the town and a dozen raiders hold their breath, waiting on you.

What does Vesper do?

Vesper steps forward to the front of the line, tail tucked, grin crooked, and calls back sweetly, "Happy to talk, Captain, but I'll do it out loud with the whole town listening, and with your orders in the Reeve's hand." She tilts her head toward Brannoc Vell and says low, "Reeve, keep your watch steady, I'm going to make her say the Sleeper's name where every neighbor can hear it."

Then, louder: "So tell us, Captain, what exactly did you want a nine-night and a key for?"

input.add_to_description: Goaded by Vesper before the Marrowmere crowd, she openly named the Sleeper and her aim: to wake the drowned wyrm at the new moon and bind it, to make Marrowmere pay tribute 'or drown'. Her men number about ten in the shrine yard; she holds a bell-shaped iron horn.

transcript.text: notebook: updated Captain Ashgrove
time: 2 minutes later: Day 2, 7:51:24 PM

It lands. Ashgrove has spent two days being the calmest person in every room, and it's a vanity as much as a habit. She can't resist an audience. The smile widens, and she steps down from the sanctuary door into the torchlight with her white glove raised like a lecturer's.

"What did I want?" Her voice carries to the back of the crowd. "The same thing every one of you has wanted, standing on mud your grandfathers dug, waiting for the river to take it back. Safety. Under this hill lies the Sleeper, a wyrm that drowned three valleys before your saints were even a rumor. At the new moon I will wake it, and it will answer to me, and Marrowmere will answer to it. Pay the tribute, and your children keep their feet dry. Refuse, and..." She spreads her hands. "The river is so very patient."

A murmur goes through the crowd, then a growl. Someone's cleaver rings on a cobble. The Reeve's knuckles are white on his boathook. "Seize her," he says quietly.

Ashgrove sighs, almost fondly. She lifts a small iron horn on a cord around her neck. "A pity you made it a public matter, Miss Thorne. I'd hoped to keep everyone *alive*." She blows one low note. From behind the shrine, from the cliff-path and the river-side, shapes rise up. More raiders, a dozen more, leather-clad with crossbows. Twenty-odd now in all, to the watch's twenty.

Crossbows come up on both sides. The yard hangs on a breath, and every eye in Marrowmere is on the girl with the horns.

What does Vesper do?

Vesper plants herself in front of the Reeve, raises both hands, and shouts at the top of her lungs so the whole hill hears: "Nobody shoot! She's got twenty men and one bluff, and she's already told you the plan, so ask yourselves who's going to be standing when the Sleeper wakes, because I just locked its door and the key is in my satchel!" She pulls the brass key out and dangles it high in the torchlight, then flashes Ashgrove her honest-looking gold eyes. "Come take it, Captain, or call off your men and keep your tea."

"DM: my spell slots are both spent, but do I still have Bardic Inspiration, and can I give a d6 to the Reeve's best crossbowman before the first bolt flies?"

Yes. Your spell slots are spent, but Bardic Inspiration is separate and you still have all 3 uses, a d6 each. Giving it takes a bonus action, and the target must be within 60 feet and able to hear you. They then have 10 minutes to spend the die on one ability check, attack roll or saving throw, adding it to the d20. Anyone in this yard who can hear you qualifies, and with your voice that's everyone.

Your shout has frozen both lines for the moment. On the watch side, Ashgrove's gaze has dropped to the key in your raised hand and stays there. The look on her face is hunger. Her horn-note called her men into the yard, but she hasn't ordered a single bolt loosed. She wants that key more than she wants anyone dead, and her crossbowmen glance at her for the word.

The Reeve's best crossbow is a lean, silent harbour-warden named Ysolt Pike, a woman with a sailor's squint, kneeling behind an upturned fish-cart with her bolt trained on the white glove. She's close enough to hear every word you say.

Do you give Ysolt the die, or someone else? And what are you doing with the key and the standoff? Ashgrove is waiting for your next word.

Vesper keeps the key dangling and her eyes on Ashgrove, but calls out in her best performer's voice, "Ysolt Pike, that's a Bardic Inspiration, a d6 for your first shot, and may the Lantern Saint steady your hand." Then to Ashgrove, sweet as honey: "Here's my offer, Captain: your men lay down their bolts and walk off this hill, and I'll hand the key to the Reeve right now, no tricks. Or you try for it, and Ysolt puts a bolt through that white glove before you reach me."

RULE Combat Step by Step:
1.  **Determine surprise.** The GM determines whether anyone involved in the combat encounter is surprised.
2.  **Establish positions.** The GM decides where all the characters and monsters are located. Given the adventurers' marching order or their stated positions in the room or other location, the GM figures out where the adversaries are/how far away and in what direction.

RULE Surprise:
A band of adventurers sneaks up on a bandit camp, springing from the trees to attack them. A gelatinous cube glides down a dungeon passage, unnoticed by the adventurers until the cube engulfs one of them. In these situations, one side of the battle gains surprise over the other.

The GM determines who might be surprised. If neither side tries to be stealthy, they automatically notice each other. Otherwise, the GM compares the Dexterity (Stealth) checks of anyone hiding with the passive Wisdom (Perception) score of each creature on the opposing side. At half past eleven you crouch in a borrowed skiff in the black shadow of the reeds, with Ysolt a dark smear on the far bank and oars wrapped in sacking. The moon is a thin pale sliver, and the river smells of mud and woodsmoke. Three miles of reed-channel lie behind you. Two shuttered lanterns hang at its bow. You count three men on the deck from here, and one on the jetty with a crossbow. Muffled laughter and the clink of cups drift from the cabin. Ashgrove laughs, a real laugh and not unkind, and steps back from the cabin door with a flourish. "Predictable, yes, and honest enough to say so. Do come in. Bring your cup. Leave the rapier on the barrel, if you'd be so kind." The sentry takes it from the barrel's lid without being asked, careful as a man handling an adder.

The cabin is clean and warm and surprisingly civil: a brass lamp, a map-table, two stools and a copper kettle on a spirit stove. Your satchel lies open on the table with the brass key glinting beside it. Ashgrove pours two cups and slides one across. Behind you the door stays open, and the sentry's boots stay in it.

"Here is my offer," she says, and sits like a woman at a bank counter. "You say the Keepers' words with me at the new moon and the door opens. The wyrm wakes and obeys. No one dies. Marrowmere pays a tithe, no more than it pays the Reeve now, and I leave it be. Your Sister goes free and unharmed, with a pension if she'll take one." She turns her cup a quarter-turn. "You, Miss Thorne, I would pay in whatever coin you name, and then you may go anywhere you like. No script. That's what you want, isn't it? A road with nobody writing the next line?"

You watch her face, the little muscles at the corners of her mouth, the steadiness of the glove around the cup. You find nothing: no tell, no flicker, no sign of a lie. She seems entirely sincere and unhurried, a woman with all the time in the world.

Neither she nor you mention the sound of oars very far off in the reeds, on the far bank, where a woman with a crossbow is waiting.

What does Vesper say?

Vesper takes a slow sip of tea, lets the silence stretch, then sets the cup down with a smile. "That's a generous offer, Captain, and I'd say yes, if you'd told me what the wyrm eats once the tithe is paid." She leans back on the stool, eyes on the key. "Humor me: what's to stop it from deciding it likes Marrowmere better than your leash, and what do you do when the first thing it does is ask for a second tithe?"

input.add_to_description: In the cabin: scimitar on her stool at her right hip, a dagger at her belt, white glove on her left hand. Besides her, a sentry at the door, a crossbowman in the rear corner by the stern window, and a third man (the mate, Harl) at the map-table. Believes the key held plus the Keepers' words binds the Sleeper like a leash.

transcript.text: notebook: updated Captain Ashgrove

Seeing needs no check. The cabin is small and the lamp is bright. Ashgrove sits across the map-table from you with her left hand, in the white glove, wrapped around the tea cup. Her right hand rests loosely on her knee, a hand's breadth from her scimitar's hilt, which is propped against the stool. A dagger rides at her belt. She hasn't touched either.

Besides her and the sentry at the door, there are two others: a crossbowman in the stern corner by the window, bolt nocked, who's been looking at you as if you owed him money, and a heavy-set man with a grey braid, bent over the map-table, who's a mate or a pilot or both. He hasn't looked up. The key lies on the table between your cups, within your reach, and not yet within anyone else's.

Ashgrove considers your question with real attention, and a flicker of something approving crosses her face. "The leash holds as long as the key does," she says, "and the words are spoken right. A key in my hand is the only thing in this world that wyrm has to fear. You're quite right that it could have ideas. That's why I'd rather it was *two* of us who knew how to stop it. You, say, with me at the new moon." She smiles. "Two guards watch each other, Miss Thorne. It's the oldest safeguard there is."

Far off in the reeds, a bird calls once, a kingfisher's note, and it doesn't sound like a bird.

What does Vesper do?

Vesper sets her cup down, lets her tail uncurl for once, and gives Ashgrove her most honest-looking gold stare. "Two guards watching each other, I like that, Captain. Let me prove I mean it." She slides one hand toward the key as if to push it across the table to her, and with the other she casts Minor Illusion from her sleeve: the sound of Corvin's drunken chorus suddenly bellowing from right outside the stern window, "Ahoy the hulk, Thack sent us!"

If every eye swings to the window, she snatches the key and goes for the open water through the stern window.

The table goes over with a crash that sounds like a dropped anvil. Tea, chart and lamp fly into Ashgrove's lap, and the lamp gutters. You vault, shoulder first, and your words come out in a breath: "...lullaby!" The sleep catches the crossbowman mid-turn. He slumps against the sill and slides down it like a sack of meal. You rolled only 18 on the dice, and that was just enough for one of them. The mate with the grey braid staggers and shakes his head, wide awake, and the sentry at the door is still on his feet.

Then there is only the window. The leaded frame bursts around your shoulder in a spray of glass and lead, and you are through it and falling, tucked tight, the key a cold weight in your sleeve. The river hits you like a slap. It is cold and black and tastes of mud, and for a long, ugly second the oilcloth drags at you. Then you break the surface under the hulk's stern, gasping, in the cover of the reeds.

You're unhurt. Above you the hulk erupts: the sentry's shout, the mate's bellow, Ashgrove's voice rising above both, no longer pleasant at all: "Boats! Lamps! She has the key!" Torches flare along the rail. A crossbow bolt smacks into the water a yard from your head.

Across the water, a darker shape on the far bank rises, and a cold, thin voice carries a long way over still water. Ysolt Pike, who has been waiting for a lantern to go dark: "Left lantern, hold your breath." There is a crack. The left lantern at the hulk's bow goes out. A second crack, and the right one follows.

The reeds are all around you, cold and thick. Shouts come from the deck above, and a skiff is being dropped. You have a key, a lute on your back, and no spells left. Corvin's decoy is still singing upriver, and your own skiff is tied at the jetty, thirty yards off.

What does Vesper do?

Vesper sucks in a breath, ducks under the surface, and swims through the reeds toward the far bank, keeping low and letting the black water hide her. "Ysolt, keep them blind, I'm coming to you!" she hisses once she's clear, then pushes through the cattails toward that dark shape, the key clamped tight in her fist.

You gain Jack of All Trades, which adds a point to every check you aren't trained in, Song of Rest, a third 1st-level slot, and your spells known are now Charm Person, Disguise Self, Sleep, Faerie Fire and Healing Word. Your slots refill with a long rest. Right now you have one left.

The *Plump Heron* slides downstream under a lightening sky, with Corvin yawning at the tiller and Piet coiling rope. You show Corvin the key in the lantern light and tell him what you saw on Ashgrove's map. By the time you've finished, his face has gone the colour of tallow. "The lower town," he says. "That's the wool quays, my warehouses, three thousand people." For once he has nothing clever to say.

At dawn you pass the Weeping Locks, stone arches beaded with moss, their great iron gates shut and dripping. A tiny lockhouse sits on the upper wall with a thread of chimney smoke. A single man in a grey coat sits on the lockhouse step, eating an apple, and he waves lazily at the barge. He might be a lock-keeper. He might be something else. You can't tell from here.

Tanner's Stair lies two hours on. The new moon is seven nights away.

What does Vesper do?

Vesper keeps her face easy and lifts a hand to wave back at the man with the apple, then murmurs to Corvin without moving her lips, "Don't slow, don't stare, and tell me if he's wearing a white glove." She sits on a bale, coils her tail, and watches the lockhouse chimney until it's behind them.

"DM: back at the Stair, how many nights until the new moon again, and does Brannoc Vell have anyone who knows how those lock gates are worked?"

Corvin squints at the lockhouse step as it slides past, then shakes his head. "No glove. Bare hands, and he's eating an apple like a man with nowhere to be." He frowns. "But that isn't Old Garrow Quill. Garrow's kept those locks thirty years. He has a bad hip and a spotted dog that barks at every hull on the river. There's no dog on that step."

The man's wave stays easy, and the barge carries you on. When the lockhouse is a grey smudge behind you, Piet lets out a breath he's been holding.

To your questions as the DM. Counting nights, you have seven left: tonight, then six more, with the new moon rising dark on Day 11. That's a week to do something about the locks.

When you reach the Stair, Brannoc Vell does have someone. Tamsin Reeve's mother, Dame Ines Reeve, is a retired lock-master who ran the Weeping Locks before Garrow Quill took over. She lives in the Tanners' Row almshouse, near enough to the stair to reach in an hour. Corvin mentions her as he's coiling a line. "She knows every gate, sluice and chain on that river. Cantankerous. Won't talk to wool merchants."

The sun is climbing, and the lower town's chimneys come into view, along with the shrine on its hill. You have one spell slot, a key, and seven nights.

What does Vesper do?

Vesper grins at Corvin. "Cantankerous and won't talk to wool merchants? Then I'll talk to her, and you'll wait at the Stair, friend." She stows the key deep in her pack beside the silver bowl and checks the oilcloth cloak.

"At the Stair I'm going straight to the almshouse to find Dame Ines, and I'll bring her a gift: Tamsin's good news that he's alive and mending. Piet, could you run ahead to Mags's and fetch Odalie and Tamsin to meet me there?"

Piet is off the barge before the plank is down, pelting up Tanner's Stair with his shirttails flying. Corvin tips an imaginary hat as you leave. "I'll be here, with a flask and a long list of things I'm not afraid of."

Tanners' Row is a crooked lane of lime-pits and drying frames, and the almshouse sits at its end: a long low building of yellow brick with a green door and a row of geraniums that someone cares about more than the roof. You knock, and a small, fierce woman answers, with white hair in a bun, a lock-master's iron whistle on a cord and a face like a closed gate. Her eyes go from your horns to your wet coat and back. "If you're selling, no. If you're from the Reeve, the answer is still no."

You say Tamsin's name. Her face changes in a heartbeat, and her hand finds the doorframe.

"Alive?" she says. "That boy. That fool of a boy." She sits down on the step quite suddenly. Then the gate shuts again, and she looks up at you with eyes like flint. "All right. He's alive. Now say what you want, because nobody comes to my door for gratitude."

Behind you, down the lane, hurrying footsteps: Odalie, in a borrowed shawl, helped along by a limping Tamsin, with Piet trotting ahead.

You have the key, the lock-master of the Weeping Locks on her own step, and seven nights.

Vesper crouches to Dame Ines's eye level and drops the performer's voice entirely. "Dame Ines, a woman named Ashgrove means to open the Weeping Locks at the new moon and drown the lower town, and a man who isn't Garrow Quill is sitting on your old lockhouse step eating an apple. Dame Ines listens with her hands folded and her mouth a hard line. When Odalie and Tamsin reach the step, she doesn't look at them. She puts her whole attention on you, and when you stop, she nods once.

"An apple on my step," she says. "Garrow would no more let a stranger sit there than he'd let one drink from his cup. Someone's got him." She spits neatly into the geraniums. "Listen, girl. The Locks have two great gates, upper and lower, and each is worked by a windlass-wheel in the lockhouse. The wheels don't turn without the sluice-pin: a bar of black iron in two halves, one half kept by the keeper, the other by the Reeve's office. Put the halves together, drop the pin in the wheel-housing, and the gates answer a strong back. Without the pin, they answer nothing. A man can't break them without a week and a hundred men, and the river would tell the whole town what he was at." Her eyes narrow. "So your Ashgrove wants Garrow's half, or the Reeve's, or both."

You ask about the whistle. She touches the iron on its cord. "It calls the lock crews, forty years of habit. Every bargee on that river knows the note, and the dog too. Biscuit comes to the name and to the whistle, so he'll bark whoever's about before they know it. If he's alive."

Tamsin, leaning on a doorpost, speaks for the first time. "Mother. Vell has the other half in his strongbox at the Quay house. If Thack knew..." He stops, and the colour leaves his face. "Thack was the Reeve's deputy. He had the strongbox keys."

Nobody speaks. Then Dame Ines says, very quietly, "Then we go to the Quay house first. And then we go to my locks."

Seven nights are left, and the Reeve's half of the pin may already be gone.

What does Vesper do?

Vesper stands and holds out an arm to help Dame Ines up. "Then we move now, Dame, and I'll take the Reeve's quay house at a walk, not a run, so nobody watching sees us worry." She turns to Odalie and Tamsin. "Sister, stay here with Tamsin, and keep that door barred."

"Dame Ines, bring your whistle. If Biscuit is alive, I want him barking when we reach the locks. And if the strongbox is empty, I'd like to know who in the Reeve's office saw Thack take the keys."

You walk the long way, past the fish-stalls and the cooperage, with Dame Ines on your arm like an aunt with a bad knee. Nobody looks twice. The Quay house is a squat grey building with a green lamp over the door and two bored watchmen on its step. The Reeve himself isn't there. He's asleep upstairs, his clerk says, with orders to wake him for nothing less than fire or flood.

"Flood," says Dame Ines. The clerk, a nervous young man named Perrin Sallow, wakes the Reeve.

Your eye catches the strongbox before anyone has said a word. It's an iron-banded chest under the clerk's desk. The brass lock is scratched, bright little furrows in the tarnish, like a mouse had been at it with a pick. But it is still locked, and the scratches stop short of the keyhole's edge, as if whoever did it had been interrupted. You tell Perrin to open it. Inside, wrapped in oiled cloth, lies a short bar of black iron, notched and split lengthwise, the Reeve's half of the pin.

Dame Ines lifts it and closes her eyes briefly. "Still here. Thank the Lantern." She wraps it, tucks it into her bodice and glares at the room. "Garrow's half is the one they want, and it's in the lockhouse, with a man who isn't Garrow."

Brannoc Vell comes down the stairs in his shirtsleeves, grey-faced and unshaven. He takes the situation in one look and says only, "How many do you need?"

The new moon is seven nights off. There is a stranger on the lockhouse step, a lock-master who wants her locks back, and half a pin.

What does Vesper do?

Vesper keeps her voice low. "Not many, Reeve, just quiet ones: Ysolt Pike and four of your steadiest watchmen, no tabards, in a fish-cart and a net-barge so we look like a catch coming up the river."

"I'll take the bank path with Dame Ines and her whistle, and I want that man with the apple to hear Biscuit bark before he thinks to look at us." She turns to the Reeve. "DM: do I have a long rest before dusk to get my spell slots back, or should I cast Charm Person on the stranger with only one slot left?"

You sleep like the dead in a cot behind the Reeve's ledger-room, with the smell of ink and tar in the blankets and the noise of the Quay a long way off. Nobody wakes you, because nothing moves at the lockhouse. Perrin Sallow brings a boy up twice with messages and sends him away both times.

You wake at a quarter to six with the light going amber in the high window, clear-headed and whole. You have all 15 hit points, all three 1st-level spell slots, and all three uses of Bardic Inspiration.

In the yard behind the Quay house, the plan has assembled itself. A fish-cart loaded with barrels and nets stands ready, and a flat net-barge is moored below the steps. Ysolt Pike leans on the cart in a fisherwoman's smock with her crossbow wrapped in sailcloth. Four watchmen in plain wool lounge about it, each with a cudgel or a boathook somewhere handy. Dame Ines sits on a barrel with her iron whistle in her fist and a knotted bundle in her lap, and she's chewing something that might be pride or tobacco. Brannoc Vell stands by, chain off, a plain grey cloak over his shirt.

"Three hours upriver by barge, with the current against us," he says. "You'll make the Locks near dark, and the lockhouse will see you coming from a mile off. Think about how you want to arrive."

What does Vesper do?

Vesper ties the oilcloth cloak on and grins at the barge. "We arrive as a catch coming home: Ysolt and two watchmen on the barge singing and gutting fish in plain view, and Dame Ines at the stern with her whistle, ready to blow it the moment we're in earshot so Biscuit starts barking."

"I'll ride in the fish-cart under the nets with the other two watchmen and slip off at the bank path a quarter mile out, to come at the lockhouse from the reeds. DM: how many first-level slots do I have now, and can I see the lockhouse's windows from the bank path?"

You have all 3 first-level slots, so Charm Person, Disguise Self, Sleep, Faerie Fire and Healing Word are all open to you, and you also have your three uses of Bardic Inspiration.

The barge pushes off with Dame Ines at the stern and Ysolt at the gutting-board, laughing loudly at a joke she didn't make. The cart rattles out along the bank road with you under the nets, breathing fish and tar, and the two watchmen beside you, Dunnet and Wick, making jokes about your horns until you remind them whose scarf they're sitting on.

At about quarter to nine, with the light nearly gone and the sky a bruised plum, the cart halts. A quarter mile out, you slide off the tail and drop into the reeds of the bank path, dry, thin and rattling. From there the Weeping Locks stand black against the last of the sky: two stone arches, the great gates dripping, and the lockhouse on the upper wall, a squat stone cabin with a slate roof and a chimney that is smoking.

The lockhouse has three windows facing the bank path. Two are lit. In the left one a man in a grey coat moves back and forth past a lamp, carrying something. The middle window is shuttered. The right is dark, and a ladder lies in the grass beneath it, as if someone has been mending the sill. There's a lantern at the lock's end, and two more men sit on the upper wall. They have crossbows across their knees and are watching the river. Their eyes are on the water, not the reeds.

From behind you, thin across the dusk, comes the first faint note of Dame Ines's whistle, far downstream and drawing near.

What does Vesper do?

Vesper crouches low in the reeds and waits for the whistle's second note, watching the two crossbowmen's heads turn toward the river. As soon as they do, she creeps along the bank to the ladder under the dark right window, stays flat to the stone, and eases up to listen and peek inside before deciding anything.

The second note of the whistle floats over the water, and both crossbowmen on the wall turn their heads and their lanterns toward it. You're a flat shadow moving between the cattails. The ladder is old and dry and gives a single complaint under your hand. The wind covers it, and the wall guards don't turn. You press against the cold stone beneath the dark window and listen, and then ease an eye over the sill.

It's a small back room with a cold stove, rope coils and a cot. In the middle of it, bound to a chair with net-cord and gagged with a rag, sits an old man with a white beard, a lame hip and a thick wool coat. His eyes are open, bloodshot, furious. That has to be Garrow Quill. At his feet lies a spotted dog with a muzzle of twine and a cord on its collar, its ears pricked toward the sound of the whistle, trembling all over. A small iron collar-ring on the dog glints, and on it, tied with a bit of fishing line, is a short bar of black iron, notched and split. Garrow's half of the pin.

The door to the main room stands ajar. Through it you can see the windlass-hall: two great wheels as tall as a man, a man in a grey coat at the nearer one hauling at the spokes with a sweat-dark back, and a second man at a table with a lamp, turning something over and over in his hand: a lump of iron, roughly the shape of a pin, and not the right one. Their voices carry. "...nothing. Won't turn. Garrow's half, the old fool said it's in the keep. It's not in the keep." "Then it's on him or the dog. Check the dog." "I checked. Captain says tomorrow night, one way or another."

Nobody is looking toward you. The guards outside are watching the river. The whistle sounds a third time, nearer, and the dog begins to whine.

What does Vesper do?

Vesper eases over the sill without a sound, drops to a crouch beside the chair, and puts a finger to her lips for Garrow. She slips her dagger under the twine on the dog's collar, cuts the half-pin free into her palm, then saws through the muzzle cord and murmurs, "Biscuit, quiet, good dog, and then loud when I say so."

Next she cuts Garrow's wrists loose and whispers, "Stay in the chair and keep your hands behind you. When the whistle's next note comes, I'm going to put those two in the windlass-hall to sleep."

The whistle sounds again, nearer, sharp. You rise in the doorway, spread your fingers and whisper the lullaby into the windlass-hall. Wounded river-warden courier who reached the Drowned Lantern in Hollin Ford carrying a sealed satchel from Sister Odalie. Was sent to find the violet-skinned, horned foundling girl.

Narrow bend of the river below Hollin Ford, blockaded by a dark raider barge with a rope strung across the channel and a shallow reed slot along the bank. Vesper's Plump Heron slipped past it with a Minor Illusion distraction. Raiders called Harl among them; more barges lie farther down.

Polite, smiling raider captain who wears one white glove; leads three barges of unmarked men in boiled leather seeking the key to the undercroft beneath the Shrine of the Lantern Saint and 'the Sleeper'. Asked Sister Odalie for the key politely.

Prisoners say Ashgrove intends to arrive 'on the night of the dark moon' with the full crew, and that a signal-lamp on the lockhouse roof tells her barge the locks are hers.

Ashgrove's map shows the Weeping Locks to be opened at the new moon (nine nights after Day 2, so Day 11) to flood Marrowmere's lower town, with three barge landings pinned on the quays. Vesper must warn the Reeve and Odalie, secure the locks, and stop Ashgrove, who still seeks the Keepers' words and the key now in Vesper's hands.

Day 4: Vesper, Dame Ines Reeve (holding the Reeve's half of the sluice-pin) and Ysolt Pike with four plain-clothed watchmen in a fish-cart and net-barge plan to retake the lockhouse at dusk. Vesper rested to full slots first. Garrow Quill (and his dog Biscuit) may be held in the lockhouse cellar by the stranger in the grey coat.

Tamsin Reeve's mother, retired lock-master of the Weeping Locks, cantankerous, lives in the Tanners' Row almshouse in Marrowmere. Knows every gate, sluice and chain. Predecessor of Garrow Quill. Won't talk to wool merchants.

Told Vesper how the Weeping Locks work: the great gates are opened by two windlass-wheels in the lockhouse that need the lock-master's iron 'sluice-pin' (a bar of black iron in two halves, one kept by the keeper, the other by the Reeve's office) and the pin-chain. Her iron whistle's note carries across the whole lock and is the old signal the lock crews obey; Garrow's dog is called Biscuit and comes to the whistle and to the name. Wants to go to the locks herself.
Went with Vesper to the Quay house on Day 4 morning; Reeve's half of the sluice-pin is intact in the strongbox.
Lock-keeper of the Weeping Locks for thirty years, bad hip, spotted dog. On Day 4 dawn a stranger in a grey coat eating an apple sat on the lockhouse step in his place: Garrow's whereabouts unknown.
His spotted dog is called Biscuit. Dame Ines fears he is dead or locked up in the lockhouse cellar.

Day 4 night: seen bound to a chair in the lockhouse's dark side room, gagged and alive, by Vesper through the right window; Biscuit the dog is muzzled and tied beside him. The man in the grey coat is working the windlass-wheels, trying to force them without Garrow's half of the pin (which Garrow swallowed? no: hidden in the dog's collar).

The Harbour Reeve's office on the Grand Quay in Marrowmere. Holds a strongbox with the Reeve's half of the Weeping Locks' sluice-pin. Brannoc Vell's clerk Perrin Sallow minds it. On Day 4 the strongbox lock was found scratched but the pin-half still inside; someone tried and was interrupted by Thack's arrest.
